rules.defining publication: A benchmark srbf runs as its defining publication states it, where later copies changed it, carries no star; the set shows a note.
rules.paper vs code: Where a benchmark's paper and its authors' code or data differ, srbf follows what produced the authors' published results (their code or data) and notes the paper's version; no star.
rules.compilation code: A compilation of other authors' benchmarks (HeuristicLab, the DSO registry, ERBench's re-renderings, the GP-benchmarks table, ...) follows its own code or data where it differs from the defining publication; the note names the defining publication's version; no star. Standalone benchmark sets keep their defining publication.

instances.text: Kepler with missing axioms draws m1 and m2 on [0.5, 2], the range of the data the authors' notebook reads; their script data_gen_kepler.py draws [0.5, 3].
Weber-Fechner uses the authors' code: log(S2/S1) on the 100 x 100 grid with S1 <= S2 (5,050 points), as the code keeps them.
F7's y takes the authors' CSV grid, 30 values on [-50, 5]; the paper's Table 6 prints [-5, 5].

The 24,000 problems are VSR-DPG's files (Jiang & Xue 2024, data/algebraic_equations @b841bb3): CVGP's expressions embedded into 10 to 50 variables. srbf follows those files: inputs LogUniform(0.1, 10), where CVGP's own code samples U(0.5, 10).
Where the paper's printed ranges differ from the authors' generator (E2, E3, E9, E10), srbf follows the generator, which produced the published results.
A-32 draws its inputs on U(1, 3), as the authors' code and experiment log do; the paper's Table 35 prints U(4, 6).
Paper and code disagree on 6 of the 7 formulas; srbf uses the code's rows, which the published runs used.
Korns-15 uses the registry's own range [0, 50] on all inputs (benchmarks.csv); Korns (2011) uses [-50, 50], as srbf's Korns set does.
Neat-6 is Keijzer's harmonic number on x = 1..50, tested on x = 1..120 (Keijzer 2003); later copies differ.

srbf regenerated the functions with the generator settings stored in the authors' released model (max_exponent_prefactor 2, max_centroids 4, its operator down-sampling), which produced their published results; the paper's Table 3 prints other settings (constants from a mantissa in [0, 1] and an exponent in [-2, 2], up to 10 clusters).
Korns-13 to -15 are ERBench's renderings on 4 inputs (Korns' unused fifth input dropped); Korns (2011) fills five inputs on [-50, 50].
Korns-15 and AI Feynman 2.0's equation 12 use ERBench's narrowed boxes ('supports altered afterwards to yield valid values'); Korns (2011) uses [-50, 50] and AI Feynman 2.0 states [-1, 1].
Nguyen-9 is Uy et al.'s F9 on [-1, 1]^2 in both.
ESR's code fits H^2 as a function of x = 1 + z (likelihood.py), so srbf poses H^2; the paper speaks of H(z).

Where SRSD's own files disagree, srbf follows SRSD's code and published data: I.44.4's n on [1e24, 1e26], integer inputs on lo..hi-1, and the signs and ranges of I.29.16, B6, B7, III.15.27 and III.21.20.

Where SRSD's own files disagree, srbf follows SRSD's code and published data (I.44.4's n on [1e24, 1e26], integer inputs on lo..hi-1, the signs and ranges of I.29.16, B6, B7, III.15.27 and III.21.20).

Korns-5 to -9, Korns-13 to -15, Keijzer-5 and Vladislavleva-7 as the table and its ECJ implementation print them, which agree with their original authors (later copies differ: abs() wrappers, swapped ranges, another Vladislavleva-7).
Nguyen-9 draws its training inputs on [0, 1]^2, as the table's ECJ implementation does (Benchmarks.java); the table and Uy et al. (2011) print [-1, 1]^2.
Keijzer-6 is Keijzer's harmonic number (Keijzer 2003) on x = 1..50, tested on 1..120.
Pagie-2 follows the authors' reference code (ECJ: [-5, 5]^3, step 0.4); Pagie's thesis uses [-3, 3]^3.
GrammarVAE-1 is fitted on the authors' 1,000 evenly spaced points on [-10, 10].
Keijzer-5, Korns-7, Korns-13, Vladislavleva-7, Poly-10 and Friedman-I/II: HeuristicLab's code agrees with the defining authors (later copies differ).
Korns-14 uses HeuristicLab's sign, 22 + 4.2((cos x0 - tan x1)(tanh x2 / sin x3)) (KornsFunctionFourteen.cs); Korns (2011) prints 22 - 4.2(...).
Korns-15 draws X2 on [0, 50], as HeuristicLab's code does to avoid NaN (KornsFunctionFifteen.cs); Korns (2011) uses [-50, 50].
AircraftLift uses HeuristicLab's corrected sign, C_La (alpha - alpha0) with alpha0 = -2 (commit 50af0024); Chen et al.'s appendix prints alpha - 2.
Keijzer-6 is Keijzer's harmonic number (Keijzer 2003) on x = 1..50, tested on 1..120.
I.16.6 draws a = u/c and b = v/c as in the AI Feynman without-units data the authors point to (u, v and c on [1, 5]); the paper states (-1, 1).
Keijzer-5 samples its denominator variable on [1, 2] as Keijzer (2003) defines it; later copies swapped two input ranges.
Keijzer-6 is the harmonic number sum 1/i (Keijzer 2003, Eq. 7); later copies print x(x+1)/2.
Keijzer-4, -8 and -9 use Keijzer's own training and test grids (step 0.05; tests starting at 0) where later copies differ.
Korns-7 uses Korns' (2011) amplitude 213.80940889; later copies print 2.1380940889.
Korns-5, -6, -8 and -9 use plain log and square root as Korns prints them; later copies wrap the arguments in absolute values.
Korns-13 to -15, dropped from later copies, are included, Korns-15 on Korns' range [-50, 50].
For bulk modulus srbf uses the 450 rows the paper reports on; the preprocessing script writes 504 rescaled rows.
The released code runs 97 of the 100 equations; srbf runs all 100, as the paper's results table does.
Four formulas are printed with typos in the paper; srbf uses the forms the authors ran (their repository).
The rule |y| < 100 is the authors' code; no paper states it.
Neat-9 (the Pagie function) is sampled at random on [-5, 5]^2, as the neat-GP paper samples its training sets; Pagie's own 26 x 26 grid is in 'Pagie (fixed points)'.
Neat-6 is Keijzer's harmonic number on x = 1..50, tested on x = 1..120 (Keijzer 2003); later copies print x(x+1)/2.
Nguyen-9 and Nguyen-10 sample their inputs on [-1, 1]^2 as Uy et al. (2011) define them; later copies use [0, 1]^2.
Pagie-1 is fitted on the authors' 26 x 26 grid with step 0.4 on [-5, 5]^2.
Differential rotation uses the notebook's seeded 27/7 split, which produced the published result; the paper speaks of 28 of 34 points.
Wave interference fixes E2 = 3.5, as the authors' script does (the constant the demo discovers); the paper's Table 10 lists E2 as an input on [1, 5].
The black-body photon count uses h = 6.123, as the authors' script does; the paper prints h = 6.626.
Poly-10 samples its inputs on [-1, 1] as Poli (2003) defines it; later copies use [0, 1].
srbf uses sigma = 50, 40 and 30, which the authors' plotted curves and reported errors match; the printed panel titles give 1/30, 1/40 and 1/50.

The three FDE problems use the boxes and formulas of the authors' generators (HeuristicLab), which produced the data (Flow psi with sin(pi theta/180)); the paper's tables print wider input spaces and sin(theta/(2 pi)).
Sine is sin(x) on the 63 points x = 0, 0.1, ..., 6.2 as the Field Guide defines it; later copies replaced it with another formula sampled at random.

Ripple2d is 2 sin((x1 - 4)(x2 - 4)) as its author defines it; later copies misprint it.
Vladislavleva-7 is 2 sin((x1 - 4)(x2 - 4)) as Vladislavleva et al. (2009) define it; later copies print 2 sin(x1 - 4)(x2 - 4).
Keijzer-6 is Keijzer's harmonic number (Keijzer 2003) on x = 1..50, tested on 1..120; later copies print x(x+1)/2.
